chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Malik ibn Atiyya, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who was contracted (mukatab) to pay for his freedom, who died without having paid off his contract, and left behind wealth and children. He (peace be upon him) said: If his master, when he contracted him, had stipulated upon him that if he was unable to pay one of the installments, he would be returned to slavery, and he had indeed been unable to pay an installment, then whatever he left of anything would be for his master, and his son would be returned to slavery if he had a son before the contract. And if he contracted him later and did not stipulate upon him, then his son is free, and he would pay on behalf of his father whatever remained upon him from what his father left. And there is nothing of the inheritance for his son until he pays off what is upon him. So if his father had not left anything, then there is nothing upon his son.

key_terms.الْمِيرَاثِ: Inheritance; the share of the estate left by the deceased.
key_terms.رَدٌّ فِي الرِّقِّ: Returned to slavery; the status of reverting to being a slave.
key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has contracted with his master to pay a specific sum for his freedom in installments.
key_terms.مُكَاتَبَتَهُ: The contractual amount or debt owed by the mukatab for his manumission.
key_terms.نَجْمٍ: An installment or portion of the contracted price.

ai.seo_question: What happens to the children and estate of a deceased contracted slave who hasn't paid off his freedom price?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the legal status of a mukatab's estate and offspring upon death, emphasizing the contractual stipulation (shart) as the decisive factor in determining whether the master retains ownership of the children and assets. It highlights the Shia juristic principle that pre-contract children remain free and liable for the father's debt from the estate, whereas post-contract children or those under a 'return to slavery' clause do not inherit until the debt is cleared. This ruling underscores the interplay between manumission contracts and inheritance law in classical fiqh.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad and Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Al Hassan Bin Mahboub, from Malik Bin Atiyya who said,

‘Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> was asked about a contracted man who died and had not paid off his contractual amount, and left wealth and children. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If his master, when he contracted him, had placed a condition upon him that if he was frustrated (from paying it off) a part of his deficit, so he would be returned in the slaver, and he was frustrated from paying the deficit. So whatever something he left, so it would be for his master, and his son would be returned in the slavery if there was a child of his before the contract. And if he was contracted afterwards and there was no such condition placed upon him, so his son is free, and he would pay off on behalf of his father whatever remained upon him from what his father had left. And there is nothing from the inheritance for his sons until he pays off what was upon him. So if his father had not left anything, so there is nothing upon his son’.
